newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Australia airlifts nationals, Cambodians worry.
newsitem.headline: Australia airlifts nationals, Cambodians worry.

text.p: The first of six scheduled Australian military flights lifted foreigners out of the tense and strife-torn capital Phnom Penh on Friday as Cambodians expressed concern over the wave of departures from their country.

About 400 to 500 people were expected to leave on the C-130 Royal Australian Air Force flights en route to Penang, Malaysia, including mostly Australians but also about 70 Canadians and a handful of New Zealanders, Swedes and Britons, embassy staff said.
Several thousand foreigners have left Cambodia since Phnom Penh's battered airport reopened on Tuesday.
As the aircraft took off, more than 100 anxious Cambodians pressed against the airport gates to watch the tourists, diplomats, aid workers and business people leave the troubled country.

Many Cambodians said they were afraid that foreigners, whose aid donations made up half the national budget and whose work has supplied thousands of sought-after jobs to Cambodians, would not be coming back.
"I came to see the foreigners leave," said Muth Sum, 40, an office worker at Phnom Penh University, which he said remained closed on Friday.
"It is not good. It's the same as 1975 and I want to leave, too," he told Reuters as he clung to the tall metal fence that blocks off the airport perimeter.
Foreigners fled the city in April 1975 as Khmer Rouge guerrillas closed in on the city. More than a million people died under their rule over the next three years and eight months.
"Our staff think we're not coming back. They're traumatised," said one foreign business woman.

Cambodians at the airport said they were devastated by the events of last weekend, when forces loyal to powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen battled First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's men in the city streets, ousting Ranariddh and leaving 58 dead and up to 200 wounded.

Hun Sen denied staging a coup, but the events have led several foreign governments to evacuate their nationals or recommend they leave the country. But most Western embassies were assuring their nationals that the situation in Cambodia was relatively safe and careful to call the exodus a voluntary departure and not an evacuation.

"This is filling a gap that commercial flights aren't filling," said an Australian Embassy official of the still limited international air service available from Phnom Penh. "This is called a voluntary, assisted departure, not an evacuation."
Some Australians said they intended to come back when Cambodia's future was more certain.
Grace Owolade, a 23-year-old from London who was working in Phnom Penh as an editor for non-profit groups, said she did not want to leave.
"I don't want to go. But there won't be much work for me now, so I'll stay away for a while," she told Reuters before boarding a camouflage-painted plane.
